passages.happening: “As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away” (verses 1-4).
passages.hearers:
Peter was an apostle, yet he calls himself ‘a fellow elder’. He stands beside the local leaders, not above them. And he names what gave the apostles their authority: he was ‘a witness of Christ’s sufferings’. He had seen it.

‘Be shepherds’ is the same verb the risen Jesus used when he told Peter, ‘Shepherd My sheep’. Peter now passes that charge on. And he reminds them whose flock it is: ‘God’s flock’, not theirs.

Then three warnings, each a temptation leaders face in every age. Not ‘out of compulsion’, serving because they must. Not ‘out of greed’: the churches supported their leaders, and some would be tempted to profit from it. Not ‘lording it over’ people, using the role to control. Instead: willingly, eagerly, and by example.

And one promise. Christ is ‘the Chief Shepherd’, a word found only here in the New Testament. Every elder answers to him. When he appears, they will receive ‘the crown of glory’. Winners of athletic games in the ancient world wore wreaths of leaves that soon withered. This crown ‘will never fade away’.
passages.ot:
Shepherd was an old picture for leadership, and for God himself: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1).

Ezekiel condemned Israel's leaders for feeding themselves instead of the flock: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). “Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty” (Ezekiel 34:4).

And God promised better ones: “Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jeremiah 3:15).
passages.hard:
What if a church leader does the opposite of what Peter describes, using the role to control, to profit, or to harm?

Peter's words are a standard leaders are held to, not a shield for them. He forbids exactly those things: greed, compulsion, lording it over people. Elders answer to the Chief Shepherd, and to the flock that is God's, not theirs.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: If you lead in any way, ask whether you serve willingly, eagerly and by example, or out of duty, gain or a wish to control. Ask whose flock you are tending. And whatever your place, ask how you can help your leaders be the shepherds Peter describes.

passages.happening: “Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
Peter speaks first to younger people, asking them to respect the elders. Then he turns to everyone: ‘clothe yourselves with humility toward one another’. Humility is not only for the young or the led. It is for all, leaders included.

The reason is a line from Proverbs, which James also quotes: God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

‘Humble yourselves ... under God’s mighty hand.’ In the Old Testament God's ‘mighty hand’ brought Israel out of Egypt: “Then the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (Deuteronomy 26:8). To bow under that hand is not giving up. It is trusting the hand that rescues, and waiting for ‘due time’ when God will lift up.

Then one of the most loved verses in the Bible. ‘Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.’ The word for ‘cast’ is used for throwing something onto another, as a load is put on an animal to carry. And the reason is not a rule. It is God's care. These readers had real reasons to be afraid. Peter does not tell them their fears are silly. He tells them where to put them.
passages.ot:
Peter quotes Proverbs 3:34, following the wording James 4:6 also uses: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (verse 5). The psalms say the same: “Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly; but the proud He knows from afar” (Psalm 138:6).

‘Cast all your anxiety on Him’ echoes a psalm: “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken” (Psalm 55:22).
passages.hard:
If we are told to cast all our anxiety on God, is it a lack of faith to keep struggling with anxiety, or to get help for it?

No. Peter's command is an invitation, not a rebuke. It rests on God's care, and it was spoken to people facing real dangers. Casting anxiety on God is something believers do again and again, not once and for all. The psalms are full of faithful people pouring out fear to God.

This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask where pride shows in how you treat others. Ask what anxiety you are carrying that you have not handed to God, and say it to him plainly. And ask who could help you carry it, since God's care often comes through people.

passages.t: The roaring lion, and the God of all grace
passages.happening:
“Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering” (verses 8-9).

“And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you. To Him be the power forever and ever. Amen” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Commands come in pairs here: be sober and be alert; resist and stand firm.

Lions still lived in the lands of the Bible, and people knew them as hunters that went for the lone or the weak. The picture warns believers not to wander off alone. The devil is real and hostile, but he is resisted ‘standing firm in your faith’, together.

And they are not alone in suffering. ‘Your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.’ The churches of Asia Minor were part of a family spread across the world. Knowing that others stood in the same place gave strength.

Then the promise, one of the warmest in the letter. The suffering is ‘for a little while’. The glory is ‘eternal’. And God will do four things himself: restore, secure, strengthen, establish. Four strong words, one after another, for people shaken by suffering: God himself will make them stand.
passages.ot:
The roaring lion is an old picture of enemies: “They open their jaws against me like lions that roar and maul” (Psalm 22:13). In Job, Satan says he has come “From roaming through the earth” (Job 1:7).

And the promise of strength renewed is Isaiah's: “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).
passages.hard:
Does the roaring lion mean that every hardship, illness or low mood is an attack of the devil?

Peter does not say so. He speaks of a real enemy who wants to devour faith, especially when believers are suffering and isolated, and he calls them to resist by standing firm together. He does not teach that every trouble has a demon behind it, or that sickness and sadness are signs of spiritual attack to be fought by prayer alone.

Some Christians have been told that their depression or anxiety was ‘the enemy’ and that they only needed to resist harder. That burden is not from this verse. Peter's own answer to suffering is God's care (verse 7), a church family around the world (verse 9), and God's promise to restore (verse 10). If sadness has settled on you and will not lift, these verses do not shame you. When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask where you are most likely to wander off alone. Ask whether you remember that believers around the world share your kind of struggle. And ask what in you needs restoring, securing, strengthening and establishing, and bring it to the God of all grace.

passages.happening:
“Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (verse 12).

“The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark. Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Peter sums up his whole letter in one line: ‘this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.’

Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, who travelled with Paul. ‘Through Silvanus’ may mean he carried the letter, or helped write it, or both.

‘The church in Babylon’ is most likely the church in Rome. Ancient Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and carried God's people into exile. After Rome destroyed Jerusalem again in AD 70, Jewish writers began to call Rome ‘Babylon’, and Revelation does the same. Early Christian tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life. A few take ‘Babylon’ literally, as the old city in Mesopotamia or a fortress town in Egypt, but few hold those views. The name fits the whole letter: God's people as exiles, with the empire's capital as their place of exile.

‘My son Mark’ is almost certainly John Mark, whose mother's house in Jerusalem was where Peter went after he escaped from prison. Peter calls him ‘my son’ in love. Early writers said Mark wrote down Peter's memories of Jesus.

‘A kiss of love’ was a greeting among family and close friends. The church adopted it as a sign that believers were one family. And the last word is ‘peace’, for all who are ‘in Christ’.
passages.ot:
Babylon is the city of Judah's exile. The psalm remembers it with grief: “By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Psalm 137:1).

And the prophets told the exiles to hold on to God there, as Peter tells his readers to stand firm: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles” (Jeremiah 29:7).
passages.asks: Ask what you would say if you had to sum up your faith in one line. Ask whether you are standing firm in grace or in something else. And ask whom you could greet, this week, as family in Christ.
